prompt: Quitanda's reports make the orders database slow, so someone proposes turning on Multi-AZ. What will that change for the reports?
hint: Can the standby be queried?

choices.text: Nothing: the standby takes no connections
choices.why: Right. Multi-AZ is insurance against a failure, and commits get slightly slower, not faster.

choices.text: They get faster, because reads are shared between the two zones
choices.why: Every read still goes to the primary; the standby only receives writes.

choices.text: They move to the standby automatically, leaving the primary to the shop
choices.why: Nothing is ever routed to the standby until a failover makes it the primary.

choices.text: They read data that is a few seconds old
choices.why: That describes a read replica, which is asynchronous and readable.

prompt: After a Multi-AZ failover, what must Quitanda's application do to reach the database again?
hint: The address of the instance is a DNS name.

choices.text: Switch its configuration to the standby's own endpoint
choices.why: The standby has no endpoint of its own; the instance's name is moved to it.

choices.text: Reconnect to the same name, which now points at the standby
choices.why: Right. Which is why a client must not cache the DNS answer forever.

choices.text: Wait for the old primary to be repaired, since RDS fails back automatically
choices.why: The standby becomes the primary and a new standby is built; nothing waits for the old machine.

choices.text: Nothing: open connections move across with the data
choices.why: Every open connection breaks, and transactions in flight are rolled back.

prompt: In moto, `reboot-db-instance --force-failover` succeeds and the instance stays in `sa-east-1a`. What can you conclude about your application's failover?
hint: What did moto build when `--multi-az` was set?

choices.text: That it reconnects within the documented 60 to 120 seconds
choices.why: Nothing was failed over, so nothing about reconnecting was measured.

choices.text: That moto failed over and back again within the call
choices.why: There is no standby in moto: `SecondaryAvailabilityZone` is `None`.

choices.text: That failover is disabled on this instance and must be turned on
choices.why: The instance is `MultiAZ: True`; moto simply models no standby.

choices.text: Nothing; only a rehearsal on a real account measures it
choices.why: Right. moto accepted the request and simulated none of what it asks for.

prompt: A PostgreSQL `db.m7g.large` is 0.442 USD an hour Multi-AZ and gp3 is 0.438 per GB-month Multi-AZ. What does a Multi-AZ instance with 50 GiB cost in a 730-hour month? Give USD to two decimal places.
What does a Multi-AZ DB cluster give Quitanda that a Multi-AZ instance does not?
hint: Count the copies, and ask what each does while it waits.

choices.text: Two copies that answer reads, and a faster documented failover
choices.why: Right. Two readers behind a reader endpoint, and a failover AWS documents as typically under 35 seconds.

choices.text: Writes on all three instances at once
choices.why: There is one writer; the readers receive its writes.

choices.text: Support for every RDS engine, Oracle and SQL Server included
choices.why: The cluster is for PostgreSQL and MySQL only.

choices.text: Protection against a `DELETE` without a `WHERE`
choices.why: Every copy receives the delete; only a backup undoes a mistake.

prompt: In a Multi-AZ DB cluster a commit waits for one of the two readers, not both. What does that buy, and what does it cost?
hint: Think about the slower reader.

choices.text: It buys nothing; both readers are always identical
choices.why: The reader that did not acknowledge can be a moment behind.

choices.text: A slow reader does not hold up commits, and a read from the reader endpoint may be slightly old
choices.why: Right. The acknowledging reader has everything, which keeps failover safe.

choices.text: Commits become asynchronous, so the cluster can lose transactions on failover
choices.why: One reader always has every committed transaction, and that is the one failed over to.

choices.text: Writes go to whichever reader answers first
choices.why: Writes go to the writer; the readers only acknowledge.

prompt: Someone runs `DELETE FROM orders` without a `WHERE` on the primary. What does the read replica hold a moment later?
hint: A replica replays whatever the primary commits.

choices.text: The rows, since replicas ignore deletes
choices.why: A replica replays every change, deletes included.

choices.text: The rows until someone promotes it
choices.why: Promotion stops future replication; the delete has already arrived.

choices.text: No rows either: it replayed the delete
choices.why: Right. A replica is not a backup; point-in-time recovery is what undoes this.

choices.text: The rows, because it is a day behind
choices.why: Replica lag is usually seconds, not a day, and it is not a safety margin.

prompt: A customer places an order and the confirmation page, which reads from a replica, says "no orders yet". What is the fix the lesson gives?
hint: Which reads can afford to be a moment old?

choices.text: Add more replicas, so one of them is up to date
choices.why: Every replica is asynchronous; more of them do not remove the lag.

choices.text: Read from the primary on the page that follows a write
choices.why: Right. Reports can be seconds old; a customer reading their own write cannot.

choices.text: Make the replica synchronous with `--multi-az`
choices.why: That flag adds a standby that cannot be read; the replica stays asynchronous.

choices.text: Give the replica a larger instance class than the primary
choices.why: A bigger replica can keep up better, and it is still behind by the time the change takes to arrive.

prompt: What does promoting a read replica do, on AWS?
hint: Can it be undone?

choices.text: It swaps the roles, so the old primary becomes the replica of the new one
choices.why: The old primary learns to follow nothing; the link is simply cut.

choices.text: It makes the replica synchronous until it is demoted
choices.why: There is no demotion; promotion is one-way.

choices.text: It cuts the link and makes a standalone instance that accepts writes
choices.why: Right, and it cannot be reversed. moto accepted it and kept the link in its records.

choices.text: It moves the primary's endpoint to the replica
choices.why: The promoted instance keeps its own endpoint; moving names is what Multi-AZ failover does.

prompt: A replica in us-east-1 receives the São Paulo primary's write-ahead log, 500 GB in a month, at 0.138 USD per GB. What does the transfer cost that month? Give USD to two decimal places.
hint: Gigabytes times the price per gigabyte.

prompt: In moto, a replica was created from an instance with `--backup-retention-period 0`. Why would AWS refuse the same request?
hint: What is a replica built from?

choices.text: Replicas need a Multi-AZ source
choices.why: A Single-AZ instance can have replicas; it needs backups on.

choices.text: Replicas start from a backup
choices.why: Right. Retention of at least one day is AWS's condition, and moto does not check it.

choices.text: Retention 0 makes the instance read-only
choices.why: Retention decides backups, not whether the instance accepts writes.

choices.text: A `db.t4g.micro` is too small to have replicas
choices.why: The refusal is about backups, not the class.

prompt: Quitanda restores its orders database to 14:32 on Tuesday. Where is the restored data?
hint: Does a restore rewind the instance?

choices.text: In `quitanda-orders`, rewound to 14:32
choices.why: The original is left exactly as it was, mistake included.

choices.text: In a snapshot that has to be restored again
choices.why: The restore already produced an instance; there is no second step to a snapshot.

choices.text: In a read replica of the original
choices.why: A restored instance follows nothing; it is standalone.

choices.text: In a new instance, at a new endpoint
choices.why: Right. Somebody then copies rows back or points the application at it.

prompt: An instance keeps 7 days of automated backups. Which restore can AWS perform?
hint: Between the earliest restorable time and `LatestRestorableTime`.

choices.text: To three days ago at 14:32:10, to the second
choices.why: Right. The day's snapshot plus the log replayed up to that second.

choices.text: To ten days ago, from the oldest snapshot
choices.why: Ten days is outside a seven-day window; moto accepted such a restore and AWS refuses it.

choices.text: To the current second, including the last minute's writes
choices.why: The latest restorable time trails by about five minutes, until the log reaches S3.

choices.text: Only to the moment of a daily snapshot
choices.why: The log between snapshots is what makes any second restorable.

prompt: A restored instance comes up and the application servers cannot connect to it. Using what the lesson says AWS documents, what is the likely cause?
hint: What did the restore command not name?

choices.text: A restore always takes a day before it accepts connections
choices.why: It takes time to build, and then it is `available` like any instance.

choices.text: It came up with the default security group, which does not let the servers in
choices.why: Right. Name the security group and the parameter group in the restore command.

choices.text: The master password was reset by the restore
choices.why: The data, users included, is as it was at the restore point.

choices.text: The servers still use the old endpoint, which now refuses them
choices.why: The old endpoint still works and still serves the original instance.

prompt: Between daily snapshots, RDS copies the engine's transaction ___ to S3 every five minutes.
hint: It is what gets replayed during a restore.

prompt: Quitanda deletes an instance that had automated backups and one manual snapshot. What is left afterwards, by AWS's default?
hint: Which of the two belongs to the instance and which to the account?

choices.text: Both, until the retention period expires
choices.why: Automated backups go with the instance unless you ask to keep them.

choices.text: The manual snapshot only
choices.why: Right. It belongs to the account and stays until somebody deletes it.

choices.text: The automated backups only
choices.why: It is the other way round: manual snapshots outlive the instance.

choices.text: Nothing: a deleted instance takes all its backups
choices.why: Manual snapshots are never deleted with the instance.

prompt: Why keep a manual snapshot before a migration when point-in-time recovery already covers the last seven days?
hint: What happens to the point in time after seven days?

choices.text: It is kept after the window moves on, until somebody deletes it
choices.why: Right. And it survives the instance being deleted.

choices.text: A snapshot restores faster, since it is replayed to the second
choices.why: A snapshot has no log beside it; it is one moment and nothing after.

choices.text: A manual snapshot is free, while automated backups are billed
choices.why: Both are billed at the backup price beyond the allowance.

choices.text: Automated backups cannot be restored into a new instance
choices.why: A point-in-time restore does exactly that.

prompt: Match each problem to the copy that solves it.
hint: One is about a machine, one about reads, one about a mistake, one about years.

pairs.left: The database must be kept for five years

prompt: Put the steps of recovering from a `DELETE` without a `WHERE` in order, keeping the writes made since.
hint: The original instance keeps running throughout.
items: Find the time of the mistake
Restore to a point just before it, naming the security group and parameter group
Query the restored instance for the deleted rows
Insert them into the original, then delete the restored instance

prompt: Which of these did moto accept in this lesson that AWS would refuse? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four numbers and conditions moto could have checked.

choices.text: A backup retention of 36 days
choices.why: Yes; AWS's maximum is 35.

choices.text: A restore to a time before the instance existed
choices.why: Yes; AWS restores only inside the window.

choices.text: A replica of an instance with backups off
choices.why: Yes; AWS needs at least one day of retention.

choices.text: A manual snapshot of a running instance
choices.why: That is ordinary on AWS too.

choices.text: A delete with `--skip-final-snapshot`
choices.why: AWS accepts it when said out loud; what it refuses is a delete with neither flag.
